title: ‘Ozempic babies’: What women need to know about fertility, contraception and pregnancy
subtitle: Reports of unexpected pregnancies have given weight-loss medicines a new nickname. Behind it are different questions about ovulation, the contraceptive pill and pregnancy safety—and women need clear answers to each.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 16 September 2026

Women taking medicines commonly discussed under the ‘Ozempic’ label face an important distinction: some treatments may improve conditions associated with difficulty conceiving, while one medicine, tirzepatide, can also reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraception. Neither finding means these medicines have been established as safe to use throughout pregnancy.

The subject is explored in ABC News’s ‘Understanding the Ozempic baby boom,’ published on 30 August, featuring fertility specialist Dr Lucky Sekhon. But the phrase ‘baby boom’ should not be mistaken for a measured increase in births caused by a drug. The evidence reviewed for this article does not establish such a population-wide effect.

For a woman hoping to conceive, an unexpected pregnancy may be welcome. For someone relying on contraception, it may disrupt decisions about her health, work and family. Both deserve counselling that begins with the medicine she actually takes.

## One nickname, different medicines

Ozempic contains semaglutide. Mounjaro contains tirzepatide. Their names are often grouped together in public discussion, but their contraceptive advice is not interchangeable.

Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro prescribing information says tirzepatide delays stomach emptying and may reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives. It advises patients using the pill to switch to a non-oral method or add a barrier method, such as condoms, for four weeks after starting treatment and four weeks after every dose increase. Non-oral hormonal contraception should not be affected.

The UK’s specialist contraception guidance does not recommend the same additional precaution simply because someone takes semaglutide. It reports no clinically relevant reduction in oral contraceptive availability with that medicine. The evidence comes from studies of drug absorption, however, rather than large trials measuring unintended pregnancies. Vomiting and severe diarrhoea can separately interfere with pill absorption; women experiencing these symptoms should follow their pill’s instructions and seek advice from a pharmacist or clinician.

## Fertility findings need careful interpretation

There is research behind the possibility that these treatments can affect reproductive health. A 2023 systematic review brought together 11 randomised trials involving 840 women with polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS. It found improved menstrual regularity and a higher rate of spontaneous pregnancy among women receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists, alongside improvements in insulin resistance and body measurements.

The limits matter. Only four included studies assessed pregnancy outcomes, treatments and participants differed, and the review found no statistically significant overall difference in total pregnancy or IVF pregnancy rates. The trials used exenatide or liraglutide, rather than establishing a fertility benefit for Ozempic specifically. These results cannot be applied to every woman struggling to conceive, or used to promise a pregnancy.

A pregnancy following treatment also cannot, by itself, show whether the explanation was a change in ovulation, contraceptive failure or another factor. Personal accounts can identify questions researchers should investigate; they cannot determine how frequently an outcome occurs.

## An unexpected positive test calls for care, not panic

Pregnancy planning requires a separate conversation. Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic prescribing information advises stopping the medicine at least two months before a planned pregnancy, because semaglutide remains in the body for an extended period. It also directs patients to discuss how blood sugar will be managed.

![A positive pregnancy test strip](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/Pregnancy_test_strip.jpg)

Contextual photograph: positive pregnancy test strip, uploaded 21 March 2007 by Klaus Hoffmeier and released into the public domain. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pregnancy_test_strip.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

For women who discover they are pregnant after exposure, the available evidence offers some reassurance without establishing safety throughout pregnancy. The UK Teratology Information Service reports that available studies have not identified increased risks of several major adverse outcomes following early-to-mid-pregnancy exposure. It also stresses methodological limitations and the fact that treatment was usually stopped early. Those findings leave important questions about longer exposure unanswered.

Its patient guidance advises women using a GLP-1 medicine for weight loss to stop when pregnancy is recognised and contact their healthcare team. Women taking one for diabetes need prompt advice about an alternative treatment plan: maintaining blood-glucose control remains essential. An accidental exposure is not, by itself, proof that a baby has been harmed.

The responsibility should not fall on women to disentangle a viral nickname from several different prescriptions. Manufacturers already publish warnings; prescribers and dispensing services need to make them understandable before treatment begins and revisit them when doses change or pregnancy plans do.

The meaningful question behind ‘Ozempic babies’ is whether women have the information and support to decide if, and when, they want to become pregnant. A headline about surprise should never replace that conversation.

The Athena Perspective.
